story:
The sandstorm had erased the expedition’s easy certainties. Across the dead communications basin, emergency beacons blinked from dune to dune, each carrying a damaged fragment of the same distress sequence. Five team members regrouped around the fragments while the buried survey station waited somewhere beyond the last marker. Since casual impressions had produced several plausible paths, the reviewers relied on the local rules and the surviving field evidence alone.

At the first beacon, the panel weighted down the governing sheet before the wind could take it. For this incident, the board declared the coherent signal bearer protocol active; ordinary rank and reputation did not count. They also fixed one shared status scale for the whole inquiry: clear counted as 0; dormant counted as 1; stable counted as 2; waking counted as 3; latent counted as 4; open counted as 5.

The tally began at 6. The auditors would examine, in order, relation, temporal, causal, spatial, sequence, and protocol evidence, using coefficients 11, 13, 5, 3, 2, and 7. At each stream they squared the current tally, added that stream’s coefficient multiplied by its status value, and retained the remainder modulo 97. They would make three passes without resetting: first in the stated order, then in reverse order with the coefficients reversed, and then in the stated order with the coefficient list rotated one place left. That complete three-pass cycle would itself be repeated 115 times. Only after the procedure was fixed did the panel open the recovered logs.

The first usable artifact was a pairing sheet, its edges stiff with sand. When it was recovered, Sawyer Okada’s team pairing stood at stable. Even the damaged roster still marked Casey Rossi’s team pairing as dormant. A clock-backed entry, protected inside a repeater housing, listed Morgan Okada’s signal interval as stable.

The investigators then followed the chain physically. The repeater response that followed Drew Nguyen registered as clear, while causal review marked Gray Meier’s repeater response open. Door and route checks placed Sawyer Okada’s beacon sector at stable; witnesses in the corridor put Casey Rossi’s beacon sector at clear. At the next marker, reconstruction kept Morgan Okada’s relay order at latent. A close photograph of the token set the auditors’ final check for that station: Drew Nguyen’s cipher glyph was latent. At final count, Gray Meier’s cipher glyph remained stable.

A second beacon had collapsed against a ridge, forcing the team to read its evidence in the order the fragments could be freed. A witness who checked the roster left Drew Nguyen with a waking team pairing. On the sealed worksheet, clerks wrote latent beside Gray Meier’s team pairing.

The timing marks survived on a strip of heat-darkened film: clocked entries put Sawyer Okada’s signal interval at dormant, while the sequence sheet showed Casey Rossi’s signal interval as waking. Downstream checks tied Morgan Okada to a latent repeater response. A movement sketch marked Drew Nguyen’s beacon sector as latent, and the route ledger tied Gray Meier’s beacon sector to dormant.

Only then did they compare the ordered logs and the equipment inventory. In the ordered log, Sawyer Okada’s relay order appeared as waking; the ordered sheet showed Casey Rossi’s relay order as clear. Inventory counted Morgan Okada’s cipher glyph as dormant.

Near the basin’s final marker, the surviving notes had to be reconciled against the instruments themselves. In the earlier pairing note, Morgan Okada carried an open team pairing. After the timesheet review, Drew Nguyen’s signal interval stayed open, while reconciled timing notes kept Gray Meier’s signal interval at latent.

The repeater’s response offered a separate trail. Instruments tracing Sawyer Okada’s action left the repeater response dormant; when Casey Rossi acted, the repeater response came back waking. Location review left Morgan Okada’s beacon sector waking. Sequence notes placed Drew Nguyen’s relay order at dormant, and at sequence review Gray Meier’s relay order stayed stable.

At the sealed equipment case, token and seal checks left Sawyer Okada’s cipher glyph at clear. The sealed check showed Casey Rossi’s cipher glyph as waking. With the last fragment catalogued, the panel could finally run every participant through the same uninterrupted tally.

The reviewers fed the six evidence streams through the stated three-pass cycle, preserving the running remainder between passes and between repetitions. For this incident, the accepted tally was 58.

The final definition was strict: the coherent signal bearer was the one person whose six-stream tally equaled the accepted tally. No reputation, proximity to the buried station, or strength of an individual beacon could substitute for that test. The panel sealed the records and waited for the calculation to identify the bearer.

Its path crossed receiving, solvent cleaning, microscopy, frame repair, quarantine, and the vault, leaving five overlapping records to be reconciled. Because ordinary impressions had made several people look plausible, the reviewers agreed to trust only the surviving incident file and the workshop’s stated audit procedure.

Before anyone compared the five names, the panel read the governing note beside the astrolabe’s custody photographs. For this incident, the board declared the certified restoration lead protocol active; ordinary rank and reputation did not count. They also fixed one shared status scale for the entire inquiry: waking counted as 0, open as 1, clear as 2, latent as 3, stable as 4, and dormant as 5.

The clerk wrote the calculation method on a fresh card. The local tally began at 7. In order, the six streams were relation, temporal, causal, spatial, sequence, and protocol, carrying coefficients 2, 5, 11, 13, 3, and 7. At each stream, the panel squared the current tally, added that stream’s coefficient multiplied by its status value, and kept the remainder modulo 97. It made three passes: first in the stated order, then in reverse order with the coefficients reversed, and then once more in the stated order with the coefficient list rotated one place left. Without resetting the tally, it repeated that complete three-pass cycle 116 times. Only then would the surviving records be allowed to speak.

The pairing sheet emerged from beneath a tray of solvent labels. Harper Okada’s apprentice lineage stood at dormant, while the damaged roster still marked Harper Ortiz’s apprentice lineage as waking. No one trusted the contrast until a witness checked the paper fibers and the matching signatures.

Those notes sent the auditors back to the rooms themselves. Door and route checks placed Harper Okada’s workshop room at dormant; corridor witnesses put Harper Ortiz’s workshop room at open.

The treatment sequence was reconstructed from the microscopy queue, where Sawyer Patel’s order remained waking. Finally, a close photograph of the token set placed Winter Meier’s tool stamp at latent, and the final count left Tatum Novak’s tool stamp clear. The fragment’s wrong tray now looked less like a mistake than a warning against trusting any single record.

A roster witness brought the next clue from the quarantine desk: after checking the names against the surviving apprenticeship notes, Winter Meier’s apprentice lineage stood stable. On a sealed worksheet, clerks had written latent beside Tatum Novak’s apprentice lineage. The two entries were logged separately, their seals intact.

The clocks supplied a different kind of pressure. Clocked entries put Harper Okada’s work interval at waking, while the sequence sheet showed Harper Ortiz’s work interval as dormant. Downstream testing then tied Sawyer Patel to a latent chemical response. The movement sketch added that Winter Meier’s workshop room was latent, and the route ledger tied Tatum Novak’s workshop room to clear.

At the ordered-log cabinet, Harper Okada’s treatment order appeared clear. Harper Ortiz’s treatment order was stable on the ordered sheet. Inventory, less forgiving than recollection, counted Sawyer Patel’s tool stamp as dormant. The investigators pinned each document beside the room where it had been made, resisting the temptation to turn the pile into a simple list of suspects.

The earlier pairing note had survived only because it was folded inside a frame-repair estimate; it showed Sawyer Patel carrying an open apprentice lineage. A timesheet review kept Winter Meier’s work interval clear, while reconciled timing notes left Tatum Novak’s work interval latent. The three records disagreed in tone, but not in the fact that each had been made during the astrolabe’s passage through the workshop.

Instruments tracing Harper Okada’s action left the chemical response clear. When Harper Ortiz acted, the chemical response came back stable. Location review then left Sawyer Patel’s workshop room stable, narrowing the route through receiving and solvent cleaning without settling the larger question.

Sequence notes placed Winter Meier’s treatment order dormant. At sequence review, Tatum Novak’s treatment order stayed latent. The last checks concerned custody: token and seal checks left Harper Okada’s tool stamp stable, while the sealed check showed Harper Ortiz’s tool stamp open. The panel set those results beside the damaged tray and prepared the final calculation.

By evening, the astrolabe rested in the vault under quarantine notation, and every disputed mark had been tied to a room, an instrument, a witness, or a sealed sheet. The panel ran the prescribed passes without resetting the tally between them. For this incident, the accepted tally was 64.

The final definition was strict: the certified restoration lead was the one person whose six-stream tally equaled the accepted tally. No title on a timesheet, confident testimony, or apparent importance in the chain of custody could replace that test. The auditors closed the file with the names, statuses, and calculation preserved for verification.
